items.text: Grief for the self who deserved support earlier is real grief. It doesn't disappear when relief arrives. It circles back. Both things happen at once, sometimes in the same hour.
items.rationale: Names the cyclical, non-linear co-existence of grief and relief after late diagnosis — the part the public conversation consistently misses. Backs Mair et al. 2026 without overstating it.

items.text: The late-diagnosis conversation talks a lot about relief. Less about the grief that comes with it — for the years without support, for the self who never got to be explained, for relationships strained by difference nobody named.
items.rationale: Different entry into neurogrief: lists the specific objects of grief rather than the emotional cycle, earning recognition through concrete specificity rather than abstraction.

items.text: AuDHD isn't autism + ADHD added together. The traits can blend into something neither diagnosis fully describes — wanting routine and novelty at the same time, for instance.
items.rationale: Uses the paradox example (routine and novelty simultaneously) to make the abstract 'third neurotype' claim concrete and immediately recognisable to the community.

items.text: The 'I have both' framing misses something: in AuDHD, some autistic and ADHD traits fuse into entirely new colours. What comes out the other side isn't one or the other. It's its own thing.
items.rationale: Challenges the dominant additive framing with the tie-dye metaphor transposed into plain language. More confrontational than post 3 — invites productive pushback.
items.sensitivity_flag: Source is a practitioner-authored community article, not peer-reviewed research. The tie-dye model is attributed to Craddock 2024 but is not clinical consensus — frame as a useful lens, not an established finding.

items.text: 88% of PDA parents report being blamed for their child's behaviour — most often by teachers and clinicians. The people doing the hardest caregiving, being told they're the problem.
items.rationale: Leads with the hard stat, closes with the emotional reality behind it. No softening — respects the reader's intelligence and the weight of the finding.

items.text: If every professional encounter left you feeling like the cause — not just unsupported, but accused — that is a failure of the system. Not evidence you're doing it wrong.
items.rationale: Speaks directly to the PDA parent whose internal narrative has become shame. Recentres accountability on the system without lecturing about the system.

items.text: When a PDA child can't go to school, 'won't' is the wrong word. The nervous system has declared the environment unsafe. That's not defiance. That's survival.
items.rationale: The 'can't not won't' reframe is clean and quotable. Physiological framing challenges the default 'behaviour to manage' narrative without moralising.

items.text: 7 in 10 neurodivergent employees don't know what accommodations they're legally entitled to. Written instructions instead of verbal. Async meetings. Flexible formats. These are rights, not favours.
items.rationale: Pairs the Understood 2026 stat with three concrete, non-obvious examples. 'Rights, not favours' is the frame shift that makes it shareable and actionable without veering into advice.

items.text: 72% of neurodivergent employees mask at work because it feels necessary. What would actually have to change for it to feel safe to stop? Not in a perfect world. In your actual workplace, next week.
items.rationale: Drops the stat then pivots to a specific, grounded question — 'next week' pushes against abstract wishful answers and is designed to generate real responses, not just agreement.

items.text: The app that promises to rescue your executive function still costs executive function to run. A system you have to maintain might spend more than it saves.
items.rationale: Names the unspoken irony in ADHD productivity culture without moralising. Framed as provocation drawing on lived experience, not a data claim, which is the only honest way to publish this given thin sourcing.
items.sensitivity_flag: No peer-reviewed backing for the net-cost claim. Sourcing is thin — practitioner blogs with commercial interests. Publish as a provocation grounded in community resonance only. Do not add statistics or present this as a finding.

items.text: Unmasking isn't just stopping the performance. For people who masked for decades, there's a harder question: who were you when nobody was watching? What if you lost track of that person?
items.rationale: Shifts the masking conversation from exhaustion (common territory) to identity erosion (underexplored). The question form invites reflection without prescribing an answer.

items.text: Long-term masking doesn't only hide who you are. After enough years, it can leave you genuinely unsure what your real preferences even are. That's not weakness. That's what masking costs.
items.rationale: Complements post 11 by naming the outcome explicitly — uncertainty about one's own preferences — and reframing it as a structural cost of masking rather than a personal failing.
